lines: A company replicates its entire lakehouse bucket to a second region, every single night, and calls that disaster recovery.
Then a real regional outage hits, and the catalog database turns out to have never been backed up at all.
Every table's actual data survived the outage perfectly.
None of it points at anything a reader can actually use.
Worth pausing on this before it gets answered.
Every single file that lived in the primary bucket now also sits safely in the secondary region.
Does that mean the table itself is safe?
Or is there something a table needs that a bucket copy alone never actually provides?
steps.answer: No, the data alone isn't the table. A table is its data plus the metadata that locates and describes it, and a bucket copy only ever moves the first half of that.

lines: Here's the first specific thing that metadata copy leaves behind.
A table's manifest doesn't store a loose hint about where its files live -- it stores a fully qualified path.
Copy the bucket's bytes into a new region without rewriting that manifest, and every single path still names a location in a region that's gone.
Only once the manifest itself is rewritten to the new region's own paths does the replicated data become reachable again.
steps.takeaway: Replicated bytes at an old absolute path are unreachable until the manifest is rewritten to match.

lines: Here's a second, entirely separate thing a bucket copy never touches.
The catalog database is the system that answers which manifest belongs to which table in the first place.
It lives outside the bucket entirely, so a job that replicates bucket bytes has no reason to ever back it up.
Lose that catalog, and a table's files can be sitting there completely intact while nothing in the system can say where to even look.
steps.takeaway: A table's data can survive perfectly and still be unfindable, because the catalog that locates it is a different system.

lines: One more question worth sitting with before the reveal.
The encrypted bytes themselves made the trip to the secondary region without any trouble.
Does the key that encrypted them need to make that same trip?
Or is ciphertext something that travels safely on its own, key or no key?
steps.answer: Yes, the key absolutely has to travel too. Ciphertext without its matching key is just noise, and a key that only ever existed in the failed region leaves every replicated byte permanently unreadable.

lines: Here's that failure demonstrated directly, on the exact same encrypted bytes both times.
A key that's scoped to a single region simply fails to decrypt anything once that region is gone.
A key that's genuinely multi-region is, by definition, the same key material sitting in both places at once.
Handed that same ciphertext, the multi-region key decrypts it without any trouble at all.
steps.takeaway: A key that only exists in the failed region turns every replicated byte into unreadable noise.

lines: Now picture the worst version of this problem: the attacker isn't outside the system, they're holding valid admin credentials.
Against an ordinary backup, those stolen credentials are enough to delete the only copy that was left.
Against a compliance-mode, write-once backup, that exact same delete request gets refused, from that exact same admin, until its retention period has genuinely run out.
The protection isn't about trusting fewer people with access -- it's about surviving the moment the access itself has been stolen.
steps.takeaway: Immutable backups exist for the moment someone with full, legitimate access is the attacker.

lines: All of this only matters if the recovery targets behind it are actually real numbers, not aspirations.
A recovery point target and a recovery time target are both just claims on a page until somebody actually restores something and times it.
A regulation like DORA turns that restore drill from an occasional nice-to-have into a standing, recurring obligation for the organizations it covers.
The regulator isn't inventing a new idea here -- it's making the one honest proof of a recovery plan routine instead of theoretical.
Pulling the whole picture together now.
Recovery point and recovery time targets get set per tier, the same way an earlier topic tiered its freshness targets.

Four separate systems -- the manifest's paths, the catalog, the encryption key, and a replicated stream's own offsets -- each need their own recovery plan, because a bucket copy only ever covers one of them.
And none of those plans are proven until a real, timed restore actually meets the target it was supposed to meet.
steps.takeaway: Bucket replication answers one of four questions a real disaster recovery plan has to answer.

lines: One real test to close on, run against real local files and a real encryption key rather than just described.
A manifest's absolute paths are shown breaking after a simulated region move, then genuinely working again once those paths get rewritten.
A key that's scoped to just one region is handed a real piece of ciphertext to decrypt.
Does it somehow manage to decrypt that ciphertext anyway, or does it fail exactly the way the claim predicts?
steps.answer: It fails exactly the way the claim predicts, with a real decryption error raised on real ciphertext. Only the key that's genuinely shared across both regions decrypts that same ciphertext without issue.
